chunks.text:
#### What should I do if flood water has already reached me?

Stay calm. Stay above water. Defensive swim.

- Get to the highest point above water that you can.
- Grab floating objects to help stay afloat.
- Use your arms to keep your head above water.
- Avoid debris, vehicles, or anything that could trap or crush you.
- Swim or float toward rooftops, trees, or high stable structures.
chunks.sectionPath: During (React) > For Adults

chunks.text:
#### How do I defensive swim in a flash flood?

Float on your back with your feet up pointed downstream.
- Use your legs as bumpers to push off obstacles.
- Spot calm water or a safe shallow spot — swim hard towards it and crawl to get out.
chunks.sectionPath: During (React) > DEFENSIVE SWIM: Float on your back with your feet up pointed downstream.

chunks.text:
#### What are the four immediate emergency actions during a flash flood?

1. Get to higher ground. If you live in a flood prone area or are camping in a low lying area, get to higher ground immediately.
2. Obey evacuation orders. If told to evacuate, do so immediately. Lock your home when you leave and disconnect utilities and appliances.
3. Practice electrical safety. If water covers the electrical outlets or if cords are submerged, do not go into that room. If you see sparks or hear buzzing, crackling, snapping or popping noises, it is not safe to enter the room.
4. Avoid flood waters. Remember, it only takes six inches of moving water to knock you off your feet.

Turn around, do not drown! Do not drive in flooded roadways or around a barricade.
chunks.sectionPath: During (React) > DEFENSIVE SWIM: Float on your back with your feet up pointed downstream.

chunks.text:
#### How do I safely walk through flood water if I have no other choice?

FLOOD WATER IS EXTREMELY DANGEROUS. WALKING IN FLOOD WATER SHOULD BE A LAST RESORT.

Avoid danger:
- Protect your legs and body as much as you can. Wear long pants, boots, or sturdy shoes if you can.
- Use a stick to help stabilize each step. Probe ahead for unstable ground, holes and objects.

Moving flood water: Face upstream. Shuffle sideways.
1. Get into a sturdy stance, face the water coming towards you (upstream).
2. Aim diagonally toward the safe place.
3. Walk sideways using small steps.

HIP WADERS CAUTION: If you fall in fast moving water, the waders could fill and drag you down. Remove them before entering swift moving water, or be ready to take off quickly if needed.
chunks.sectionPath: During (React) > DEFENSIVE SWIM: Float on your back with your feet up pointed downstream.

chunks.text:
#### Why should I wash flood water off as soon as possible?

Flood water is very dirty with sewage, chemicals, and diseases. It can make you very sick.
- Be sure to disinfect any wounds thoroughly and watch for any signs of infection.
- Watch for other signs of sickness if you touched or consumed flood water.
chunks.sectionPath: During (React) > DEFENSIVE SWIM: Float on your back with your feet up pointed downstream.

chunks.text:
#### What should I do with my pets if flood water is here with no warning?

1. Bring pets inside and get to the highest level of the building or home.
2. Be sure all windows and doors are closed. Choose a room away from windows in the center of the building if possible.
3. Put pet life jackets on your pets, if you can.
4. Wait until the water has passed through your area.

Keep your pets with you. Stressed pets may try to hide — this should be avoided.
- Keep them on leash. This helps keep them close and prevents them from being swept away from you.
- Bring the emergency kit and life-vests or floatation device with you.
- Listen to local radio for updates or watch the news for pet resources.
- If safe to do so, move yourself and pets to the tallest, most solid home or building you can access.
chunks.sectionPath: During (React) > Water is Here, NO WARNING:

chunks.text:
#### Where should I take my pets if a flash flood evacuation is announced?

If there is warning of an evacuation:
- Relocate pets to a safe place upstream with friends, family, an established animal emergency shelter, or pet-friendly hotel.
- Do not assume that your pets will be accepted at a human emergency shelter.
- Do not assume that human rescuers will help with pets.
chunks.sectionPath: During (React) > Water is Here, NO WARNING:

chunks.text:
#### Should I try to rescue stray animals I see during a flash flood?

Do not attempt rescue unless it is safe.
- It is often unsafe to try to rescue pets during an emergency or evacuation.
- Many rescue groups will list items in need of donation during an emergency such as food, bedding, carriers, and leashes.

If you are able, sign up to foster displaced pets. Social media groups and rescue organizations will post their needs online. In most cases you will fill out a foster application to temporarily host a lost pet.
chunks.sectionPath: During (React) > For Wildlife

chunks.text:
#### How do I know my flash flood risk and stay updated on warnings?

1. Know your area's flash flood risk. Visit FEMA's Flood Map Service Center to know types of flood risks in your area. Pay attention to flood warnings and be prepared to evacuate immediately if advised.
2. Make a flood plan. Outline where to go, what to do, and what you will need in a flood. List nearby shelters in case you must evacuate. Plan to move to higher ground before flooding begins. Call 211 for assistance finding evacuation options if needed.
3. Gather emergency supplies. Put several days' worth of supplies like nonperishable food, water, cleaning supplies, medication, and copies of important documents into a waterproof bag or container.
4. Stay updated. Sign up for alerts and warnings about severe weather from your local emergency office or weather app. Listen to the weather forecast on the radio, TV or weather app. Ensure your electronics are charged and pack a portable charger. Listen to NOAA's All Hazards Weather Radio. Monitor local weather reports. Download the FEMA mobile App for additional alerts.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > For Adults

chunks.text:
#### What general tips help me stay safe in flash flood-prone areas?

Flash floods happen quickly. Know what to do if you are in an unfamiliar environment when a flash flood happens.

- Know your proximity to rivers, streams, and dams. Stay away from the edge.
- During heavy rain, avoid underpasses, underground parking garages, and basements.
- Avoid hiking or camping if thunderstorms are predicted.
- Do not walk in water above your ankles as you can be swept off your feet in as little as six inches of rushing water.
- Turn off the electricity and other utilities if a flash flood is coming.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > For Adults

chunks.text:
#### How do I prepare my home for flash flooding?

Inspect your roof regularly for broken or damaged areas.
- If you need to renovate or replace any part of your roof, consider upgrading to a high-impact resistant option.
- Trim all dry, dead, or weak tree and shrub branches that could potentially become loose during a storm.

If a storm is on its way:
- Bring all loose items and outdoor furniture indoors.
- Clean your gutters and drainage areas to ensure water can drain from your roof.
- Close your drapes or blinds to prevent wind from blowing glass into your home.
- Cover or move breakable patio furniture.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > For Adults

chunks.text:
#### What is the difference between defensive and aggressive swimming in flood water?

When you are in flood water, your goal is to get out as soon as possible and avoid injury. Floods can have extremely strong currents that make it hard to move or stay in control of your body's movement. It is exhausting to swim in fast-moving flood water, so save your strength as much as possible.

To survive, you need to keep your head above the water and avoid dangerous debris and currents. Search for something to help you stay afloat. Grab onto something strong, like a tree trunk, to avoid being swept farther away while you wait for the water to go down or for help to arrive.

You do not need to be a strong swimmer to survive. You need to know how to defensively swim and aggressively swim, and when to use both techniques.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > For Adults

chunks.text:
#### When should I use defensive swim, and how do I do it?

Use defensive swim when:
- You are caught in the current
- You cannot get out yet
- You are trying to stay above water and avoid danger
- You are tired and need to rest while staying afloat

How to do it:
- Lie on your back, like a floating bug
- Keep your head up and your feet pointing downstream
- Use your legs to steer or bounce off obstacles
- Keep your arms out for balance
- Look around and breathe calmly

This swim keeps you facing what is coming. It buys you time to spot safe places and protect your body from injury.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > Defensive Swim: Stay Alive and Buy Time

chunks.text:
#### When should I use aggressive swim, and how do I do it?

Use aggressive swim when:
- You see a safe place and can reach it
- The water is calmer
- You are ready to escape

How to do it:
- Roll onto your stomach
- Swim hard toward the exit point
- Use strong forward strokes
- Get to shallow water, a tree, or anything solid

Do not waste energy too early. Wait until it is time to escape. When you see your chance, swim with everything you have.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > Aggressive Swim: Get Out Fast

chunks.text:
#### Should I practice swimming techniques before a flash flood happens?

Switch between defensive and aggressive swimming depending on what the water is doing. Practicing in calm water ahead of time can help you feel more confident.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > Be ready to use both.

chunks.text:
#### How do I prepare my pet for a flash flood evacuation?

Prepare pets for evacuation:
- Get your pets used to their carrier or riding in the car.
- Practice before an emergency. This makes evacuation less stressful.

Get connected to local resources before the emergency:
- Make a list of hotels or motels that accept pets.
- Put a window sticker on your home showing how many pets are inside.
- Add emergency contacts such as your vet or a safe haven location.
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > For Pets

chunks.text:
#### How can I build a community pet plan for flash floods?

- Join a local app like Nextdoor.com to stay informed and find pet-friendly resources.
- Trade contact info with neighbors.
- Make sure your pets have met your neighbors.
- Talk with trusted neighbors about helping your pets if you are not home.

Ask:
- Is there a nearby home that is taller or safer?
- Can neighbors help your pets reach that place during a flood?
chunks.sectionPath: Before (Prepare) > For Pets

chunks.text:
#### What safety precautions should I take during flash flood recovery?

- Pay attention to authorities for information on when it is safe to return home.
- Avoid driving except in emergencies.
- Wear protective clothing and boots during clean up and use appropriate face coverings or masks if cleaning mold or other debris.
- People with asthma or other lung conditions should not enter buildings with indoor water leaks or mold growth that can be seen or smelled.
- Children should not take part in disaster cleanup work.
- Be aware of the risk of electrocution. Do not touch electrical equipment if it is wet or standing in water.
- Avoid wading in floodwater as it can be contaminated and contain dangerous debris.
- Use a generator or other gasoline-powered machinery ONLY outdoors and away from windows.

Recovery and housing assistance: 211, National Disaster Hotline (1-800-985-5990), FEMA Text Service (43362).
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > For Adults

chunks.text:
#### What should I check before re-entering my home after a flash flood?

Look around outside first. Watch for loose power lines, broken gas lines, cracks in the foundation, and any other damage.

Check for structural damage. Parts of your home may be weak or collapsed. Approach doors slowly and check if porch roofs or overhangs are still supported.

Watch for wild animals. Snakes and other dangerous animals may be inside.

Smell gas or hear hissing? Leave right away and call the fire department.

Power lines down outside? Stay out of puddles or standing water near them.

Keep kids and pets safe. Do not let them near floodwater or dangerous areas.

Watch for hazardous materials like cleaning products, paint, batteries, and fuel containers. Ask local authorities how to throw them away safely.
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > For Adults

chunks.text:
#### Which food and water should I throw away after a flash flood?

Throw away anything that touched floodwater, including:
- Canned food
- Bottled water
- Plastic utensils
- Baby bottle nipples

If you are not sure if something is safe, throw it out.

Do not use possibly dirty water to:
- Wash dishes
- Brush teeth
- Cook or make drinks
- Wash hands
- Make baby formula or ice

Check with your health department for local advice on how to boil or treat water after a disaster. Floods can make water unsafe.
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > For Adults

chunks.text:
#### How do I prevent mold in my home after a flash flood?

Wet carpeting, furniture, bedding, and other items holding moisture can develop mold within 24 to 48 hours.

If an item has been wet for less than 48 hours:
- Clean with a phenolic or pine-oil cleaner (non-ammonia detergent, soap, or commercial cleaner).
- Disinfect with a 10 percent bleach solution (1 1/2 cups of bleach per gallon of water).
- Dry completely and monitor for several days for any fungal growth or odors.

People with breathing problems or who have weakened immune systems should stay away from moldy sites of flood cleanup.
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > For Adults

chunks.text:
#### What's the safe way to clean surfaces after a flood?

- Avoid stirring up dust or scrubbing surfaces.
- Clean gently the first time to remove loose dirt and microorganisms.
- Use a cloth dampened with clean water and detergent.
- After gentle cleaning, use dry tools such as a wet/dry vacuum to remove debris.
- Open doors and windows for ventilation and faster drying if possible.
- If you see mold, do not use fans or dehumidifiers until after cleaning the visible mold.
- If your heating, ventilation, or air conditioning system was submerged or affected by floodwater, have it inspected before use.

Use a sanitizer or disinfectant only on non-porous surfaces (metal, tile, sealed countertops, finished wood) that have otherwise been cleaned. Do not use on fabrics, carpet, or unfinished wood. Always read product labels and follow directions.
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > How to Safely Clean Up After a Flood

chunks.text:
#### How do I dry out my home's interior after a flash flood?

- Use portable dehumidifiers; rental costs may be covered under your flood policy.
- An air conditioner can help start the drying process.

If the walls are damaged:
- Insurance claim tip: take photographs of the baseboard, then remove it.
- Knock small holes at floor level in the drywall between wall studs to release trapped moisture and start drying.

Inspect heating and water systems:
- Have your furnace checked for damage.
- Your water heater may appear to work, but if floodwater reached part or all of the tank, the insulation inside may be damaged.
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > How to Safely Clean Up After a Flood

chunks.text:
#### How do I do laundry safely after a flash flood?

Floodwater can contain bacteria, viruses, sewage, chemicals, and asbestos. Items like mattresses, furniture, stuffed toys, and pillows must be thrown away. Nonporous fabrics such as rugs, linens, and clothing can sometimes be cleaned and saved.

Prepare for cleaning: Gather gloves, goggles, and protective clothing. If your washer or dryer was flooded, do not use it until inspected by a professional. If using a working machine, run one empty hot-water cycle with bleach before washing clothes. If you do not have a working machine, use a large bucket, kiddie pool, or bin outside for washing. Clean mildewed items outside to avoid spreading mold indoors. Wash clothes only with clean water.
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > How to Safely Clean Up After a Flood

chunks.text:
#### In what order should I take off contaminated clean-up gear after a flood?

Have nearby: disposal bags, alcohol-based hand sanitizer, and a wash bucket.

Remove items in this order:
1. Boots or shoe covers → hand sanitizer
2. Gloves → hand sanitizer
3. Hard hat → hand sanitizer
4. Goggles or face shield → hand sanitizer
5. Coveralls (touch inside only, roll inside out) → hand sanitizer
6. Mask or respirator (touch straps only) → wash hands

- Wash gear separately from other laundry using PPE-safe detergent.
- Wash heavily contaminated gear twice.
- Hang to dry indoors or in shade; do not leave in direct sunlight.
- Sanitize your wash bucket or machine with bleach and water before and after use.
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > How to Safely Clean Up After a Flood

chunks.text:
#### How do I bleach-launder clothing contaminated by flood water?

Wear gloves and goggles. Throw away dry-clean-only clothes, wool or leather items, and anything with foam padding (like bras or shoes).

1. Wash clothes and fabrics outside before using a machine to avoid spreading mold spores. Never mix liquid chlorine bleach with ammonia, vinegar, or acids (creates toxic gas). Use only EPA-registered liquid chlorine bleach (not color-safe bleach):
- Measure 2/3 cup bleach per 1.5 gallons of water.
- Add cool water first, then bleach.
- Submerge clothes and agitate with a long-handled tool to cover all areas.
- Soak for several minutes, then rinse thoroughly.

2. Wash again with laundry detergent.
3. Dry on the highest heat or hang in direct sunlight to kill bacteria.
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > How to Safely Clean Up After a Flood

chunks.text:
#### What emotions are common during and after a flash flood?

During and after a dam or levee failure and flood, many people experience:
- Panic/feeling out of control
- Anger
- Generosity toward others
- Despair
- Anxiety/uncertainty
- Disorientation
- Cooperation/teamwork with those around you
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > How to Safely Clean Up After a Flood

chunks.text:
#### When does the emotional toll of a flood usually hit hardest?

The full force of the emotional toll will hit after the floodwaters recede. That's when exhaustion sets in. As people look at their real losses, they may experience grief, desperation, and depression.

- Pay attention to your own and others' emotional responses once the emergency crews leave.
- Talk with others to find solidarity and ease stress. Pain from loss and tough times can be eased when people keep talking with each other.
- Ask for help! Many people are around who want to help and will help. They just need to know what to do that will be most helpful right now.
- Take care of your physical and emotional needs. Eat a balanced diet to fuel your energy. As much as possible, get enough sleep.
- Couples who are facing losses may find that each spouse copes differently with the stress. No one reaction is right. The important thing is to keep talking things over and to show love and affection toward each other.
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > Coping After

chunks.text:
#### Should I reach out to a flood survivor even if I don't know what to say?

As people put their lives back together, what matters most is friends, neighbors, and families supporting each other.

When people stop talking with others who have suffered loss or who are facing financial trouble, they send the message that they don't care. Keeping in touch with the people who are hurting doesn't mean you have to have the answers. Just giving someone a chance to talk about the problem can be an important step in healing.

If you are the survivor wondering why friends haven't called, understand that rather than feeling indifference, friends and neighbors may just be caught up in their own losses, uncertainties, and problems. Those who were not hurt directly by the floods may feel guilty and not know what to say. It is ok to call your support system to let them know you are in need of their support.
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > We all need someone to care.

chunks.text:
#### How can I safely feed an infant after a flash flood contaminates the water?

SAFEST — Use safe water:
- Bottled water is best.
- Use unboiled bottled water (table, spring, or mineral water) or distilled water to make a baby feed, but you must give the feed to the baby immediately.
- Use ready-made formula milk as an alternative to powdered feeds.

2nd safest — If using tanker water: Boil it!
- Do not use unboiled tanker water.
- Boil and cool for 30 minutes in a clean, covered container, then follow the instructions on making the feed.
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > For Kids

chunks.text:
#### How can I make a DIY water filter if I can't boil water after a flash flood?

Ways to filter and purify water with a homemade filter:
1. Get two plastic water bottles and cut off the bottom of one of them. Start from the top half of the bottle.
2. Add a piece of tissue, shirt, sock, or any kind of cloth that can help hold the charcoal in place.
3. Add sand.
4. Add gravel or pebbles.
5. Add water.
6. Give it at least an hour to filter into the other unused water bottle before drinking it.

Other purification options: UV light purifiers, disinfecting tablets, commercial filters, activated charcoal. You can make your own charcoal by making a campfire, covering it with dirt and ash, and allowing it to cool completely. Once cooled, crush it into small pieces.
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > For Kids

chunks.text:
#### How can I help kids regain a sense of security after a flash flood?

Kids may see changes in their parents and think that they are somehow to blame for increased tension. Talking together and being honest yet reassuring about problems the family faces can help children feel more in control.

If money is tight, parents can ask children to help think of ways the family can work together to keep expenses down. Parents need to be sure children don't blame themselves for tough economic times.
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > For Kids

chunks.text:
#### How do I reunite with a pet I was separated from during a flash flood?

Stay tuned to local news and social media groups to learn where displaced pets may have been taken.
- Contact your local emergency manager to learn about next steps.
- Report your pet missing on every local lost and found listing you can find. An internet search will help you find these groups and sometimes new ones specific to the dam failure emergency. If an individual or group is holding on to your pet they are looking for you too.
- Stay connected with social media. Shelter, rescue, neighborhood, and emergency groups will often post pet updates here.
- Gather photos, microchip number, and vet records for your pet so you can prove ownership.
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > For Pets

chunks.text:
#### What physical stress signs should I watch for in my pet after a flood?

Physical signs of stress or anxiety in pets:
- Self-mutilation — excessive paw-licking or chewing
- Diarrhea
- Vomiting
- Anorexia
- Panting
- Eliminating in the house or outside of the litter box
- Straining to urinate or not passing urine (cats)
- Twitching when sleeping
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > How Pets May React to This Event

chunks.text:
#### What behavioral changes might my pet show after a flash flood?

Behavioral changes:
- Hiding
- Avoidance of triggers
- Freezing
- Restlessness
- Pacing
- Destruction of surroundings
- Aggression
- Anxiety
- Depression
- Avoidance of people
- Refusing to repeat any activities experienced during the emergency, such as car rides or kenneling
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > How Pets May React to This Event

chunks.text:
#### What symptoms in my pet require a vet visit after exposure to flood water?

If your pet was exposed to flood water or was missing during a dam failure, watch for breathing changes:
- Breathing faster than usual
- Working hard to breathe
- Coughing
- Discharge from the nose and/or eyes

Monitor them during potty breaks or in their litter pan for diarrhea or loose stools, blood in the stool, or vomitus near their urine or stool.

Medical changes needing veterinarian care as soon as possible: breathing changes, frequent vomiting or diarrhea, loss of appetite, straining to urinate or not passing urine. Mild diarrhea or poor appetite should be closely monitored for worsening — if not improved within two days, take them to the vet.
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > How Pets May React to This Event

chunks.text:
#### How can I help my pet recover behaviorally after the flood trauma?

Whether your pet experienced the emergency event or was in a safe place during a dam failure, stress can result. Extreme conditions, separation from their guardian, being kenneled near other pets, or handling or transport with strangers can all be traumatizing to your pet.

- Be patient with pets recovering from traumatic events.
- Do not rush them into activities they are resisting, even if these used to be tolerated or enjoyed.

Consult with your veterinarian for behavioral changes that are severe or affecting quality of life, such as aggression, fear of handling, or peeing/pooping inside the house or outside of the litter pan. Your vet may recommend the help of a veterinary behaviorist, who will likely use a combination of behavioral therapy and medications.

Good rule of thumb: If you are unsure what happened to the pet, consult your vet. Getting a professional to examine your pet can ensure unseen injuries do not get worse and helps your pet heal faster.
chunks.sectionPath: After (Recover) > How Pets May React to This Event
